summary.title: 67 Weird Debugging Tricks Your Browser Doesn't Want You to Know
summary.one_liner: You learn many non-obvious browser DevTools techniques, such as using conditional breakpoints as logpoints, tracing call stacks, timing code, and inspecting elusive DOM elements.
takeaways: Conditional breakpoints can simulate logpoints (console.log without pausing) in browsers that lack them, and console.count adds a running count.
Watch expressions and DOM mutation breakpoints can snapshot localStorage or the DOM each time execution pauses.
console.trace inside a conditional breakpoint helps find the caller of an unpaired call, such as a show without a matching hide.
Console APIs like console.time, copy(), getEventListeners($0), and monitorEvents($0) help with timing, extracting data, and inspecting events.
Setting a debugger call via setTimeout lets you inspect elements that vanish on mouse hover.
summary.summary: This article is a list of non-obvious browser debugger hacks, aimed at readers with intermediate or higher devtools knowledge. It shows how to use expressions with side effects inside conditional breakpoints to log, count, trace call stacks, time code, change program behavior, and sample executions. It also covers console utilities such as monitor, debug, copy, getEventListeners, and monitorEvents, plus techniques for inspecting HTML/CSS and elusive elements. Each trick is presented with a short code snippet and a note on when it is useful. An update notes that major browsers now support logpoints natively.
